The CRC engine operates by evaluating data streams through four distinct consistency classes—consistent, statistical, structural, and self_consistent_wrong_vs_ledger—each representing a mode of disagreement with a source of truth. The core insight is that systems can internally agree while simultaneously diverging from reality. This is modeled mathematically as a set of mappings from input data spaces to a truth manifold, where each class corresponds to a projection error type. For instance, 'consistent' maps to a scenario where all projections align but differ from the ground truth; 'statistical' captures variance-based deviations; 'structural' identifies topological mismatches; and 'self_consistent_wrong_vs_ledger' isolates cases where internal consistency fails against external validation. These modes form a dual lattice of error types, enabling precise diagnostics without silent averaging. Each class defines a failure regime governed by specific assumptions about data independence, distributional behavior, and structural invariance. The engine thus functions as a compositional consistency checker, leveraging both empirical and theoretical constraints to detect and classify discrepancies.
